title: Chapter 8. When a tomato with your DNA heals you and is eternal life: when you eat according to your biological needs

blocks.text: In the garden, a tomato does not look like a miracle. It looks like what it is: a fruit of summer, of winter if there is shelter, of flavour when the earth and the water and the sun have done their part, and of disappointment when they have not. Pedro, however, sees in that tomato a horizon and names it with a sentence that must be handled honestly: “When a tomato with your DNA heals you and is eternal life: when you eat according to your biological needs.”

blocks.text: This chapter is not going to present eternal life as a scientific fact, or cures as a result already demonstrated. That would be to fail the truth, and Pedro is not done a favour by dressing a dream until it becomes an advertisement. The dream is the dream, and it deserves to be told as such: that of a food designed for each person's biology, able to heal and to lengthen life. Beside that dream there is a more modest and more solid present, which also belongs to him: eating according to what the body needs, with the Mediterranean diet and the garden under our feet, and with a science, nutrigenomics, that is beginning to understand how genes and foods speak to each other. The real and the dreamed will be distinguished here with clarity, so that the reader does not have to guess where one ends and the other begins.

blocks.text: The real, first. Nutrigenomics — and its sister, nutrigenetics — study the relationship between food and the genome: how certain nutrients influence the expression of genes, and how certain genetic variants mean that two people do not respond in the same way to the same dish. There are old and well-established examples, even if they were not presented under that name: whoever cannot tolerate lactose, whoever must watch their iron, whoever lives with an illness in which diet is part of the treatment. There is, also, a field under way, with studies of diets, variants and cardiovascular risk, many of them in Mediterranean populations, which still does not allow each person to be prescribed, with certainty, a menu made to the measure of their DNA. Serious reviewers say so calmly: there are clues, there are plausible interactions; what is often still lacking is replication, sample size, the diversity of populations. Anyone who today sells a test and a miracle diet from a swab is running ahead of the evidence. Anyone who investigates, by contrast, is on a real path. This book takes the path, not the shop-window miracle.

blocks.text: The Mediterranean diet, here, is not a folkloric ornament. It is the food of this shore: olive oil, vegetables, fruit, legumes, cereal, fish, nuts, wine if it is drunk, and drunk in measure, and meat, when there is meat, without being the centre of the plate. In Spain a large clinical trial was done, PREDIMED, with 7,447 people at high cardiovascular risk. The original 2013 paper had to be retracted and republished in 2018, in The New England Journal of Medicine, after problems of randomisation were corrected. In that revised version, Ramón Estruch and his colleagues still observed that a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil or with nuts was associated, in those people, with fewer major cardiovascular events than a low-fat control diet. It is not eternal life. It is evidence — with its limits, with its correction included — that the way of eating of this land, when it is truly kept up, can look after the heart. The garden, the market, the oil, the real tomato, the fish from nearby: these are not nostalgia. They are, already, a way of eating according to a shared biological need, before anyone reads a genome.

blocks.text: And there are tomatoes, already, that science has changed. They should be named without being confused with the tomato of the dream.
blocks.html: And there are tomatoes, already, that science has changed. They should be named without being confused with the tomato of the dream.

blocks.text: In 2008, Eugenio Butelli, Cathie Martin and their team, in a paper in Nature Biotechnology, described a tomato that accumulated anthocyanins — the pigments of blueberries and blackberries — by expressing two transcription factors from the snapdragon, Antirrhinum majus. The fruit turned purple, in the flesh as well, and its hydrophilic antioxidant capacity was multiplied. In a pilot test, Trp53⁻/⁻ mice, which are susceptible to cancer, lived longer if their diet was supplemented with those tomatoes. That last sentence must be left in its place: it is a result in a particular animal model, not proof that that tomato lengthens human life, or that it cures a cancer in people. Years later, the Del/Ros1-N variety, from Norfolk Plant Sciences, completed in 2023 a voluntary consultation with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA, file BNF 000178). The agency, with the data presented, raised no further questions then about human food derived from that tomato, beyond the producer's usual responsibilities. A purple tomato rich in anthocyanins exists, then, in the laboratory and on regulatory ground. It is not a tomato “with your DNA.” It is a tomato with a reinforced pigment pathway.

blocks.text: In 2022, Jie Li and colleagues, also in the orbit of the John Innes Centre, published in Nature Plants a tomato edited with CRISPR-Cas9. By knocking out the Sl7-DR2 gene, the fruit and the leaves accumulated 7-dehydrocholesterol, provitamin D₃, which ultraviolet B light can convert into vitamin D₃. The plants went on growing. The leaves, after exposure, reached high concentrations of the vitamin; the fruit, lower concentrations, but no longer none. It is a new route, still of research, towards a food biofortified in a vitamin that many people lack. It is not a universal cure, either, or a personalised tomato. It is a clear example of what gene editing can already do in a garden crop: not invent eternity, yes enrich an everyday food.

blocks.text: The dreamed, now, without disguising it. Pedro imagines a further step. Not a tomato for everyone, but a tomato — or a loaf, or a vegetable — thought out for one person's biology: for their DNA, for their lacks, for what their body does not know how to make or how to use. A food that does not only nourish, but heals. And, at the end of that path, eternal life. One may smile. One may, also, listen to what the sentence asks beneath its excess. It asks that food cease to be only a commodity and become care again. It asks that the garden and the laboratory not turn their backs on each other. It asks that the abundance of the earlier chapters not be translated into more shelves full of what is not needed, but into what is right for each organism. It asks, at bottom, not to die altogether quite so soon, which is a very old and very human request, and which science has not granted, and which this book will not grant on its behalf.

blocks.text: Eternal life, here, is the largest name of a wish: to live longer and better, to fall ill less, not to have to buy health in instalments as one buys everything else. The tomato “with your DNA” is the image of a food that knows you. Neither of those things has been demonstrated. Both may guide a research and a garden, if they are not passed off as a result.

blocks.text: In the meantime, what can already be done can be done, and it is not little. Eating from the garden when one can. Cooking with good oil, with vegetables, with legumes, with fish from nearby, with the tomato that tastes of tomato, purple or red, of ancient genetics or of the laboratory, but real. Listening to the body. Listening, with caution, to what nutrigenomics goes on confirming, not to what an advertisement promises. Leaving eternity on the shelf of dreams, in sight, so as not to forget it, and not selling it as if it were already on the plate.

blocks.text: At dusk, a tomato of this land still warm from the sun does not cure death. It nourishes. Sometimes, it cheers. At the table of the Mar Menor, that is already a beginning. The rest, if it comes, will come by science and by care, not by a miracle this book cannot sign. Pedro's dream remains written, entire, so that it will not be lost. The science, beside it, so that it will not be confused.

blocks.text: A precaution, in closing, for the reader in a hurry to believe or to doubt. Nutrigenomics does not ask for faith; it asks for studies. The purple tomato and the vitamin D tomato do not ask for worship; they ask to be looked at for what they are: advances of the laboratory and, in one case, a food that has passed a regulatory consultation, not a panacea. The Mediterranean diet does not ask for an altar; it asks for a table. And Pedro's dream does not ask anyone to swallow it as if it were a result: it asks to be allowed to live beside the garden, as a compass, not as a certificate. Whoever today eats according to what their body needs is already, in part, inside this chapter. Eternity can wait. Lunch cannot.
